title: The Stoic morning
hookLine: preview, one principle, and a clear intention

lines: THE ALARM, THE PHONE, THE HEADLINES.
DECIDED BY WHOEVER GOT THERE FIRST.
cards: The alarm goes off, and the phone is already in reach. Before feet touch the floor, a thumb is scrolling: messages, headlines, someone's vacation, a work email marked urgent.
A minute or two in, the day's mood has been set by whoever got there first. The turning year is done.
For the next stretch, the porch puts a year of Stoic reading to work in ordinary life: morning, evening, work, home, the hard days and the good ones. It starts where every day starts.

teach.h: PREVIEW: MEET THE DAY ONCE, CALMLY.
teach.b: Three parts, gathered mostly from Marcus. First, preview.

Marcus opens book two of his notebook with this, in George Long's 1862 translation: "Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial."
It sounds grim. But read on: none of them can really harm him, he says, and they're his kin, made for working together. The preview isn't pessimism.
It's packing an umbrella: when the rude email comes, you've already met it once, calmly. Second, one principle.
Marcus tells himself to keep his principles ready the way a doctor keeps instruments at hand for sudden cases. Not a whole philosophy.
One line for the day: maybe Epictetus's split, some things are up to me, some aren't, or Seneca's begin now, or one you've written yourself. Third, intention.

teach.h: INTENTION: THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.
teach.b: On a morning Marcus didn't want to get up, he asked himself what he was made for: to lie under the blankets keeping warm, or to do the work of a human being? An intention answers that for today. Not a to-do list.
A how: patient with my kids, honest in the meeting, kind on the phone. Fourth, the whole thing takes about two minutes.
Preview, principle, intention, before the phone if you can.
The day will still surprise you, but you'll meet it as yourself, not as whoever the first notification decided you'd be.

how: Some modern Stoic practitioners begin the day with a short routine drawn from Marcus and Epictetus: previewing difficulties, recalling one principle, and setting an intention.

o: a two-minute start: preview, principle, intention
a cold shower to toughen yourself for the day
an early wake-up before sunrise to work harder

games.q: the Stoic morning — tap the pairs.
p: meet the day's friction once, calmly
the work of a human being

s: Marcus's morning preview ends in contempt for difficult people
he says they can't really harm him, and that they're his kin.
Marcus admits he sometimes didn't want to get out of bed
he asks if he was made to lie under the blankets keeping warm.
the Stoic morning is a long to-do list
it's a preview, one principle and an intention about how, not what.

games.q: the alarm goes off. your hand reaches for the phone. what does a Stoic morning do first?
o: check the news to be prepared
preview the day, pick a principle, set an intention
stay in bed until you feel ready
games.why: Marcus begins by meeting the day in his mind, keeps his principles at hand, and reminds himself what he's up for.

practice: Try a Stoic morning now, whatever the hour: picture the rest of your day and meet its likely friction once, calmly. Choose one line to carry and say it silently.
Then finish this sentence for yourself, today I want to be someone who, and let all three settle.

wordCard.voice: Stoic morning: a two-minute start, preview the day, choose one principle, set a clear intention, before the world decides for you. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the rehearsal of hardships ahead, a later name for the Stoic preview.

carryVoice: Your line: preview, principle, intention. Two minutes, and the day starts as yours. Day six hundred seventy-five, done.
